## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Assakajātaka* (Ja 207) is a birth story in the Pali *Jātaka* collection [SuttaCentral]. In the narrative's frame story at Jetavana, the Buddha encounters a monk who has become lovesick and distracted by memories of his former wife [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. The Buddha informs him that this was not the first time her love had brought him misery, and relates a story of the past to illustrate the point [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879].
In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta lives as an ascetic in the Himalayas [Olson 2015; Fausböll 1879]. King Assaka of Potali is overwhelmed by grief following the death of his beautiful queen, Ubbarī, refusing to bury her and lying beside her corpse [Olson 2015]. Informed by a young brahmin, the ascetic intervenes and explains that because the queen was vain of her beauty and neglected good deeds, she has been reborn as a dung worm in the royal park [Olson 2015]. The Bodhisatta makes the worm speak to the king, and she confesses that new experiences obscure the old (*navena sukhadukkhena porāṇaṁ apithīyati*) and that she loves her worm mate far more than King Assaka [Anandajoti 2010; Olson 2015]. Disillusioned, the king casts away his grief and returns to governing [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1879]. In the story's resolution (*samodhāna*), Queen Ubbarī is identified with the former wife, King Assaka with the lovesick monk, the young brahmin with Sāriputta, and the ascetic with the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1879].
Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus records any external parallels, cross-language alignments, or Pali-internal text reuse for this discourse [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral notes four modern translations of the text in four languages [SuttaCentral].
